authorization: User: economic history feels off; no Wrigley, Mokyr, Berg? Crafts? Review and correct the economic-history reading selection.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Richard White, Railroaded (2011): corporate finance, public subsidies and political markets; selected author interview passages checked.

representative_people.context: Treats institutions, law and custom as part of economic explanation; his dispute with Menger concerns how abstraction should proceed.
representative_people.works: “Zur Methodologie der Staats- und Sozialwissenschaften” (1883; English translation 2021)

representative_people.context: Agrarian reconstruction tests legal and economic explanations against regional and documentary differences; religion/capitalism adds ethical and causal questions.
representative_people.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926)

representative_people.context: Combines medieval institutional research with personal reconstruction; distinguishes kinds of evidence and acknowledges editorial and documentary collaboration.
representative_people.works: Medieval English Nunneries (1922); Medieval People (1924)

representative_people.context: Develops institutional explanations involving rules, incentives, learning and historical paths; revises assumptions of earlier neoclassical economic history.
representative_people.works: “Economic Performance through Time” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Counts paid and unpaid production while distinguishing household forms, class and marital position. Her account of capitalist change retains maternalist assumptions and contested medieval comparisons.
representative_people.works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion

representative_people.context: Explains changes in women’s work and wages through training, household organization and industrial/agrarian change. Her qualified optimistic interpretation differs from Clark’s longer decline account.
representative_people.works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930); reprint preface (1969, signed 1968)

representative_people.context: Production relations and class conflict shape the effects of trade. The reply to Sweezy preserves interaction, contested historical stages and a concession about insufficient evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: Differential movements of prices, production and income support conjunctural inquiry. His 1956 introduction stresses uneven crises; later debate tests the model’s conditions and distinguishes his experiments from serial routines.
representative_people.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956)

representative_people.context: Sociologist and economist whose methodological polemic challenged conventional historical explanation.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903)

representative_people.context: Comparative and economic historian in dialogue with the founders.
representative_people.works: “De la méthode comparative en histoire” (1923)

representative_people.context: Quantitative economic historian whose later research connects population, nutrition, physiology and growth. The cited lecture does not verify his earlier slavery estimates.
representative_people.works: “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology: The Bearing of Long-Term Processes on the Making of Economic Policy” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Treats the market-regulated economy as historically specific; uses anthropology to examine reciprocity and redistribution and challenges Smith’s barter narrative.
representative_people.works: The Great Transformation (1944), especially chapter IV, “Societies and Economic Systems”

representative_people.context: Argues that later industrialization can differ in technology, scale, banks and state action; England’s path is not an automatic template.
representative_people.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective: A Book of Essays (1962), title essay

representative_people.context: Relates expanding demand to household labor and resource reallocation before industrialization; considers negotiation and unequal interests within households. With Ad van der Woude, presented the Dutch Republic as 'the first modern economy' (1997).
representative_people.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994); with Ad van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997)

representative_people.context: Compares developed Eurasian regions and connects European divergence with coal and overseas resources, including coercive colonial relations. These are contested explanations.
representative_people.works: The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes arguments about industrial finance and abolition; both remain contested.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Challenges the decline thesis in abolition debates; his position is not a consensus of the field.
representative_people.works: Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (1977)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes material life, ordinary markets and capitalism while allowing overlap. His world-economy chronology and reading of Weber are arguments within debate.
representative_people.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977), especially pp. 44–53, 65–67, 81–83

representative_people.context: With his co-author, critically rereads Labrousse’s experimental construction of evidence and its narrowed serial reception. This is neither rejection of every model nor unqualified defense.
representative_people.works: Grenier and Lepetit, “L’Expérience historique. À propos de C.-E. Labrousse” (1989; abstract consulted)

representative_people.context: With his co-author, critically rereads Labrousse’s experimental construction of evidence and its narrowed serial reception. This is neither rejection of every model nor unqualified defense.
representative_people.works: Grenier and Lepetit, “L’Expérience historique. À propos de C.-E. Labrousse” (1989; abstract consulted)

representative_people.context: Responds to objections to the ancien-régime crisis model by seeking conditions for theoretical justification; the checked opening does not establish the later proof.
representative_people.works: “La crise d’Ancien Régime: un essai de justification théorique” (1992), opening p. 231

representative_people.context: Investigates market conduct and crowd protest through customary norms, legitimacy and material pressures. Hunger alone does not explain the form of action.
representative_people.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century” (1971)

representative_people.context: Questions the definition of feudalism and transfer of evidence between regions; his account permits money and instability while disputing their transformative effects.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), critique; opening pp. 134–137 consulted

representative_people.context: A Japanese intervention develops the social form of labour and questions Dobb’s geographical coverage. The essay explicitly limits this discussion to Western Europe.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism: A Contribution to the Sweezy-Dobb Controversy” (1952 English translation; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Peasant research is a named resource in Dobb’s reply and Hilton’s later synthesis. The 1956 work is the Hilton context; it is not projected backward as a publication read by Dobb in 1950.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Agrarian History of England in the Thirteenth Century (1956), cited by Hilton (1973); earlier peasant interpretation cited by Dobb (1950)

representative_people.context: Craft differentiation and corporate organization offer historical resources. Dobb tentatively recalls Unwin’s contribution to his guild interpretation; the precise source of that recollection is not established.
representative_people.works: Industrial Organization in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1904)

representative_people.context: Comparative peasant movements join production, conflict, political organization and belief; outcomes and evidence differ across periods. Acknowledges Bloch while criticizing particular Power and Duby emphases.
representative_people.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Legal and agrarian scholarship informs Tawney’s reconstruction; the introduction distinguishes legal explanations from wider economic change.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Tawney credits research on enclosures and its revision of earlier evidence; quantitative uncertainty and interpretation remain visible.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Tawney identifies Savine’s agrarian research among resources for revising the historical problem; this contextual record does not summarize his whole career.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Clark credits sustained research direction; Pinchbeck credits early guidance and use of materials. These acknowledgments document teaching, not identical conclusions.
representative_people.works: Research supervision acknowledged in Clark (1919) and Pinchbeck (1930), original prefaces

representative_people.context: His 1963 preface identifies editorial reconstruction of Power’s unfinished material; it distinguishes her draft from the published wording.
representative_people.works: Preface to the tenth edition of Power, Medieval People (1963)

representative_people.context: Power credits discussion and criticism; his separate general preface sets out the series’ evidentiary policy. That preface is not her authorial statement.
representative_people.works: General preface to Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

representative_people.context: Provides transcripts/translations of Alnwick’s register and reads manuscript/proofs; Power uses documentary comparison in evaluating injunctions.
representative_people.works: Alnwick register materials acknowledged and discussed in Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

representative_people.context: Treats domestic service as labor connected to industrial change, rather than only a private relationship between mistress and maid.
representative_people.works: Domestic Service (1897), preface and chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

representative_people.context: Compares Chinese and European economic/state trajectories, using and testing historical categories.
representative_people.works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

representative_people.context: Explains coffee-surplus destruction as support for income and employment and links crisis to the domestic market; this is retrospective historical analysis.
representative_people.works: Formação econômica do Brasil (1959), chapters XXXI–XXXII opening in2005edition

representative_people.context: Welcomes Furtado’s income-flow analysis but asks for structural explanation of wage labour and Brazil’s place in the formation of capitalism.
representative_people.works: Review of Formação econômica do Brasil (1961),277–279

representative_people.context: Explains managerial enterprise through coordination at greater throughput; the selected opening contrasts earlier market specialization with later institutional change.
representative_people.works: The Visible Hand (1977), selected Part I and chapter1 opening

representative_people.context: Distinguishes technological novelty, adoption and incremental improvement while treating invention as socially and economically situated.
representative_people.works: “The New Economic History and the Industrial Revolution” (1999), selected passages

representative_people.context: Compares changing artisanal industries in colonial India with other industrializing regions; distinguishes employment totals, organization, productivity and uneven outcomes.
representative_people.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

representative_people.context: Her study of older British manufactures provides a directly cited resource for Roy’s account of productivity and organization beyond spectacular inventions.
representative_people.works: The Age of Manufactures, 1700–1820, second edition (1994),40, through Roy (1999),8/note12

representative_people.context: Questions what railroad social-saving measures establish and how their counterfactual cost assumptions work.
representative_people.works: “Railroads, American Growth, and the New Economic History: A Critique” (1968), opening and notes

representative_people.context: Co-author with Temin of a methodological criticism within quantitative economic history.
representative_people.works: Comment on Fogel and Engerman (1979),213–214

representative_people.context: With David, challenges inference from revenue comparisons to technical efficiency.
representative_people.works: Comment on Fogel and Engerman (1979),213–214

representative_people.context: Fogel’s collaborator in contested slavery productivity research and subsequent replies.
representative_people.works: “Explaining the Relative Efficiency of Slave Agriculture” (1977), opening; Reply (1980), metadata only

representative_people.context: Defines involution, more output at diminishing returns per workday on family farms, and involutionary commercialization in North China and the Yangzi delta, drawing on Geertz, Chayanov and Boserup; Pomeranz rejects it and Huang answers (2002–2003).
representative_people.works: The Peasant Economy and Social Change in North China (1985); The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta, 1350–1988 (1990); “Development or Involution in Eighteenth-Century Britain and China?” (2002)

representative_people.context: Treats household consumption as both economic and social; inventory totals are incomplete measures of wealth.
representative_people.works: Consumer Behaviour and Material Culture (1988/1996), preface and introduction

representative_people.context: Provides a named challenge about whether apparent occupational or urban ownership patterns reflect wealth.
representative_people.works: The Pre-industrial Consumer (1990), discussed by Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix

representative_people.context: Investigates agricultural labour through colonial records while distinguishing caste labels from actual occupation.
representative_people.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

representative_people.context: Economic historian of industrialization, growth and population change. This complements his demographic, quantitative and social-history work; these are overlapping practices.
representative_people.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988); Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010)

representative_people.context: Real wages in Chinese, European, Japanese and Indian cities, 1738–1925, with Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden: Yangzi delta labourers no better off than in Beijing or Canton, and below England; Chinese cities on a par with central and southern Europe.
representative_people.works: “Wages, Prices, and Living Standards in China, 1738–1925” (2011)

representative_people.context: Historical national accounts with Guan and Li dating the Great Divergence to about 1700, earlier than the California School proposed but later than older accounts.
representative_people.works: with Hanhui Guan and David Daokui Li, “China, Europe, and the Great Divergence: A Restatement” (2021)

representative_people.context: With the UCL team, traces the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into British life and argues that gender and race shaped capital formation.
representative_people.works: with Draper, McClelland, Donington and Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (2014)

representative_people.context: Class structure and property relations, not population or trade, explain divergent agrarian paths in England, France and eastern Europe; against the demographic model of Postan (1976–82).
representative_people.works: "Agrarian Class Structure" (1976); "The Agrarian Roots of European Capitalism" (1982)

representative_people.context: The British standard-of-living debate of the 1950s and Industry and Empire (1968), which readers credit with recasting the economic history of industrial Britain; no economic text of his is read here.
representative_people.works: “The British Standard of Living 1790–1850” (1957); Industry and Empire (1968)

representative_people.context: Railroaded investigates corporate finance, subsidies and freight markets. This contribution is grounded in White’s 2011 author interview, not inferred from citation counts.
representative_people.works: Railroaded: The Transcontinentals and the Making of Modern America (2011)

strands.title: Historical economics and disciplinary institutions
strands.focus: Historical specificity and institutional research; formation of a field does not establish one doctrine.
strands.works: Schmoller’s methodological review (1883); Cunningham’s textbook (1882); Ashley and disciplinary institutions

strands.title: British economic and social history
strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.
strands.works: Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix and notes17,20

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account and the publisher excerpts of Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11); People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread.
strands.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.
